CHAPTER XXIII. A WOMAN OF BULIKA

I turned aside into an alley, and sought shelter in a small archway. In
the mouth of it I stopped, and looked out at the moonlight which filled
the alley. The same instant a woman came gliding in after me, turned,
trembling, and looked out also. A few seconds passed; then a huge
leopard, its white skin dappled with many blots, darted across the
archway. The woman pressed close to me, and my heart filled with pity. I
put my arm round her.

“If the brute come here, I will lay hold of it,” I said, “and you must
run.”

“Thank you!” she murmured.

“Have you ever seen it before?” I asked.

“Several times,” she answered, still trembling. “She is a pet of the
princess’s. You are a stranger, or you would know her!”

“I am a stranger,” I answered. “But is she, then, allowed to run loose?”

“She is kept in a cage, her mouth muzzled, and her feet in gloves of
crocodile leather. Chained she is too; but she gets out often, and sucks
the blood of any child she can lay hold of. Happily there are not many
mothers in Bulika!”

Here she burst into tears.

“I wish I were at home!” she sobbed. “The princess returned only last
night, and there is the leopardess out already! How am I to get into the
house? It is me she is after, I know! She will be lying at my own door,
watching for me!--But I am a fool to talk to a stranger!”

“All strangers are not bad!” I said. “The beast shall not touch you till
she has done with me, and by that time you will be in. You are happy to
have a house to go to! What a terrible wind it is!”

“Take me home safe, and I will give you shelter from it,” she rejoined.
“But we must wait a little!”

I asked her many questions. She told me the people never did anything
except dig for precious stones in their cellars. They were rich, and had
everything made for them in other towns.

“Why?” I asked.

“Because it is a disgrace to work,” she answered. “Everybody in Bulika
knows that!”

I asked how they were rich if none of them earned money. She replied
that their ancestors had saved for them, and they never spent. When they
wanted money they sold a few of their gems.

“But there must be some poor!” I said.

“I suppose there must be, but we never think of such people. When one
goes poor, we forget him. That is how we keep rich. We mean to be rich
always.”

“But when you have dug up all your precious stones and sold them, you
will have to spend your money, and one day you will have none left!”

“We have so many, and there are so many still in the ground, that that
day will never come,” she replied.

“Suppose a strange people were to fall upon you, and take everything you
have!”

“No strange people will dare; they are all horribly afraid of our
princess. She it is who keeps us safe and free and rich!”

Every now and then as she spoke, she would stop and look behind her.

I asked why her people had such a hatred of strangers. She answered that
the presence of a stranger defiled the city.

“How is that?” I said.

“Because we are more ancient and noble than any other
nation.--Therefore,” she added, “we always turn strangers out before
night.”

“How, then, can you take me into your house?” I asked.

“I will make an exception of you,” she replied.

“Is there no place in the city for the taking in of strangers?”

“Such a place would be pulled down, and its owner burned. How is purity
to be preserved except by keeping low people at a proper distance?
Dignity is such a delicate thing!”

She told me that their princess had reigned for thousands of years; that
she had power over the air and the water as well as the earth--and, she
believed, over the fire too; that she could do what she pleased, and was
answerable to nobody.

When at length she was willing to risk the attempt, we took our way
through lanes and narrow passages, and reached her door without having
met a single live creature. It was in a wider street, between two
tall houses, at the top of a narrow, steep stair, up which she climbed
slowly, and I followed. Ere we reached the top, however, she seemed to
take fright, and darted up the rest of the steps: I arrived just in time
to have the door closed in my face, and stood confounded on the landing,
where was about length enough, between the opposite doors of the two
houses, for a man to lie down.

Weary, and not scrupling to defile Bulika with my presence, I took
advantage of the shelter, poor as it was.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

I diverted into a service alley, seeking refuge within a stone archway. As I stepped into the gloom, I paused to survey the scene illuminated by the pale, indifferent moonlight. Before I could process the geometry of the space, a figure emerged—a woman, trembling violently, who froze mid-step to stare back at me. The silence stretched, taut and brittle, until a massive leopard erupted from the shadows. Its coat was a chaotic map of white fur marred by dark, irregular blotches, and it surged across the archway with predatory grace.

Instinctively, the woman pressed herself against my side, her breath hitching in ragged gasps. Pity, sharp and sudden, flooded my chest. I wrapped an arm around her rigid frame. "If that brute comes closer," I stated, my voice level despite the chaos, "I will engage it. You must flee."

"Thank you!" she whispered, her voice cracking. "Have you encountered this before?"

"Several times," she admitted, her knees buckling slightly under the weight of terror. "This is the Princess's pet. You are a stranger; otherwise, you would recognize her."

"I am a stranger," I confirmed. "Yet, is she permitted to roam freely?"

"She is confined to a cage, muzzle locked tight, paws encased in gloves of crocodile leather. She is chained, yet escapes with alarming frequency, draining the blood of any child she can catch. Fortunately, Bulika lacks many mothers." Her composure shattered instantly. "I wish I were at home!" she sobbed. "The Princess returned only last night, and the leopardess is already loose! How do I enter my own dwelling? She is hunting me—I know it! She will be crouching outside my threshold, waiting!—but I am a fool to discuss this with a stranger!"

"All strangers are not enemies," I countered, maintaining a defensive posture. "The beast cannot reach you until I have dealt with it. By then, you will be inside. You possess a roof over your head! What a ferocious gale it is!"

"Escort me home safely, and I shall grant you shelter from this storm," she pleaded.

"We must wait briefly," I instructed.

Her answers revealed a society built on stagnation and absurdity. She explained that her people subsisted solely on digging for precious stones in their cellars, remaining perpetually wealthy because labor was deemed a disgrace. Their ancestors had hoarded resources centuries ago, creating a static economy where wealth was inherited rather than earned. When funds ran low, they liquidated gemstones, convinced the earth held infinite reserves.

"But surely poverty exists?" I pressed.

"It is an abstraction we ignore," she dismissed. "When someone falls into destitution, we simply cease to acknowledge them. This is how we maintain our status. We intend to remain rich forever."

"And when the mines are exhausted? When the stockpile depletes?"

"We have untold quantities, and the ground yields endlessly," she insisted, her eyes fixed on something beyond my shoulder. "Besides, no foreign horde dares approach. They are paralyzed by fear of our Princess. She commands the air, the water, the earth—and presumably the fire. She rules absolutely, accountable to no one."

Periodically, she halted, scanning the darkness behind her with paranoid intensity. I questioned the xenophobia that permeated the city. "Why such animosity toward outsiders?"

"Their presence defiles the sanctity of our city," she declared. "We are ancient and noble compared to any other nation. Therefore, we expel all strangers before nightfall."

"How, then, can you admit me?"

"I shall make an exception for you."

"If no provision exists for housing travelers, why not build one?"

"Such a structure would be demolished, and its owner consumed by flames. How can purity be maintained unless we keep the base masses at a proper distance? Dignity is a fragile construct!"

She recounted that the Princess had reigned for millennia, wielding dominion over the elements themselves. Finally, she resolved to lead me to safety. We navigated a labyrinth of narrow passages, reaching her residence without encountering a single living soul. The building stood in a broader thoroughfare, flanked by towering structures, accessed via a steep, winding staircase.

As we ascended, her confidence evaporated. Fear seized her, and she bolted upward, scrambling up the final flights with frantic haste. I arrived moments later, only to find the door slamming shut in my face. I stood confounded on the landing, trapped in a narrow gap between opposing doors—just enough space for a man to lie prone. Exhausted and unwilling to soil the pristine air of Bulika further, I accepted the cramped shelter, resigned to the indignity of my position.
